brief.head: Forty years in four
brief.text: Paul Graham, Amit Varma said, sees a startup as a medieval trading voyage: instead of working at low intensity for forty years, work at high intensity for four. {102-C05}

brief.head: The pizza hypothesis
brief.text: Every business is a bundle of beliefs, Ajay Shah said: buy atta and Italian tomato cans, sell pizza at a profit. Testing it teaches you how the world works. {102-C03}

brief.head: Beware the buzzword
brief.text: Peter Thiel, Amit Varma said, treats buzzwords in a pitch as a warning sign: big data, cloud computing, blockchain, AI. A genuinely new idea doesn’t need one. {102-J07}

brief.head: Without Einstein
brief.text: If Einstein had not existed, Shah asked, how long before relativity? People would have got there bit by bit, but at a given moment, one creative fire matters. {102-C10}

brief.head: Just chop the tree
brief.text: Abraham Lincoln, Varma said, would spend four of six hours sharpening the axe. Too many of us spend the first four thousand hours sharpening it. {102-J06}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah make the case for starting up
lead.head: Wanted: founders. Apply within
body: Amit Varma opened the episode by translating Bruce Springsteen lyrics into Hindi for Ajay Shah to identify. Then, with “the tough part of the show” done, the hosts turned to their subject: why everyone should start a business.
This was Part 1 of a two-parter, and the hosts disagreed on only one point: how hard to commit.
## The case for owning

Shah offered three reasons. The first was competence: people work at a different level when the work is theirs. He quoted James C. Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*: “the most powerful fertilizer is the tender gaze of an owner.” {102-C01}
His other two, that a business makes you a better employee and teaches you how the world works, Varma called byproducts rather than reasons.
Varma’s own reasons were about change. The usual script, he said, runs from a degree to one career track for thirty or forty years, “and then we retire, and then we get dementia and then we die.”

Settle into one groove and you ossify, he argued, so that when the world changes nobody wants what you do. He cited Peter Thiel’s advice to Mark Zuckerberg: in a rapidly changing world, the biggest risk is not changing.
## All in, or detached?

Here the hosts parted ways. Shah favours side gigs run with detachment: low stakes, comfort with failure, many experiments. Traders who love money most, he noted, do less well, because “their hunger and their need for the money is distorting their clear thinking”. {102-C06}

Varma called detachment a fine personal philosophy, but argued that traders earn their calm by first plunging in with full passion. To believe a detached 30 per cent can beat someone else’s 100 per cent is, he said, “almost offensive” to those who throw themselves in.
Shah said he assumed your 30 per cent already reflected full mastery. Someone else will have that mastery too, Varma replied, and give everything.
## Five rules for founders
The rest was Varma’s advice, much of it drawn from founders’ clips on the Instagram account StartUp Archive.
First, prize love over like. In Paul Graham’s formulation, a hundred people who love your product beat a million who like it. {102-C07}

Second, ignore naysayers. A 1989 test audience panned the *Seinfeld* pilot. Varma’s warning: “the better your idea, the more likely it is that there will be many people telling you that it cannot be done.” {102-C08}
Third, start from inside rather than hunting for a gap in the market. Google began as an intellectual puzzle called PageRank; Facebook started in a dorm room.
Fourth, focus. Sam Altman calls it a force multiplier, and Bill Gates and Warren Buffett both named it their most important quality. The hard part, Varma said, is saying no to things you love.
Fifth, act. “Action produces information,” in the phrase of Brian Armstrong of Coinbase. Too many people never stop planning.

Varma closed with Milan Kundera’s man in a fog, who makes his road one step at a time. Look back at him from a distance, he said, and “you will see the man and you will see the road, but you will not see the fog.” {102-C13}
Everyone looking ahead is in fog, Varma said, and the only way through is to move forward. Start a business before the next episode, he urged, and “I will be so happy.”

second.label: Focus
second.head: Buffett’s empty diary
second.deck: Amit Varma on what Bill Gates learnt from Warren Buffett
body: Asked in a joint interview to name their most important quality, Bill Gates and Warren Buffett gave the same answer, Amit Varma said: focus. {102-R22}

Gates, Varma said, had learnt from Buffett how to say no. Once he asked Buffett to set up an event. Buffett opened his calendar, and it was almost blank. How did he do it, Gates asked. “I’ve learned to say no,” Buffett said. “You should also learn to say no.” {102-S08}

The lesson, Varma said, is not saying no to things you don’t want to do: even people pleasers manage that. It is saying no to things you love, which Steve Jobs told the designer Jonathan Ive on rejoining Apple. {#ive}

quote.text: I’ve learned to say no. You should also learn to say no.

second.caption: Buffett’s empty calendar

third.head: Leave A-B-C to anybody
body: Amit Varma was chatting with a friend, a huge celebrity in the creator economy whom he would not name, when he broke down everything the friend does. {102-S07}

“A B C is stuff anybody can do. I don’t understand why you’re doing it,” Varma told him. D-E-F was what only the friend could do, like the Lucknow love story he had written, a film that is “so much him”.
Time is scarce, Varma said: longevity is great, but it is not immortality. He is glad a show for a business channel never worked out, since it was not something only he and Ajay Shah could do.
Not that the door is shut. “Though if somebody comes with a shit ton of money, we are still open to it, but a shit ton of money only.” {102-J05}
third.caption: work only you can do

p2.title: Start something
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s reasons to start, Amit Varma’s rules for starting, and the one point on which they disagree

sections.label: Why start
sections.head: Owners tend better gardens
sections.caption: why everyone should start something
body: Everybody should take a crack at building one or more businesses, Ajay Shah said, especially those who think their lives are tidy and defined: the corporate slave, the university professor. A business can be anything from a side gig on Urban Company to a VC-funded firm aiming for an IPO.
His first reason was that ownership raises your game, beyond running to somebody else’s KRA. As James C. Scott put it, the most powerful fertiliser is the tender gaze of an owner. {102-R02}

His second was that running a business makes you a better employee. His third was that every business is a set of hypotheses about the world, and testing them teaches you. “So you will do twenty five things that are wrong,” he said. “But out of all of that, you will learn.” {#wrong}
## Before you ossify

Amit Varma called those two byproducts rather than reasons. His first reason was that a single career track ossifies you, and when the world changes, nobody wants the one thing you can do. He read out lines from Benjamin Franklin and John A. Shedd against the comfort zone. {102-J09}
His second was the pace of change itself, in an age of AI and automation. In Jack Welch’s words: change before you have to. {102-J10}
~ Naval Ravikant, Varma said, predicts that most companies will be startups of four or ten people that scale to a billion dollars. {102-R08}

quote.text: in a world that is changing rapidly, the biggest risk you can take is not changing.
quote.who: Peter Thiel’s advice, as told by Amit Varma

sections.label: The quarrel
sections.head: Cool head or whole heart?
sections.caption: detachment versus full commitment
body: Everyone should start something; the hosts disagreed about how. Ajay Shah, thinking of people who already have a main life, favours the side gig, where you nurture “little bubbling fires” and experiment with them.
Detachment, he said, means the gig is not your all-consuming passion and you are comfortable with failure. Low stakes oppress you less, so you think more coolly.
Finance has a whisper of this, he said: the traders who love money most do less well. {102-C06} He added that “if you’re a little detached, you’re playing chess, you’re playing a game”.
## Plunge first
Amit Varma was “completely on with detachment as a personal philosophy”. But detached traders, he argued, know trading so well because they once plunged into it with full passion.
To think that a detached 30 per cent of your time can beat someone else’s 100 per cent struck him as arrogance. {#thirty}

Shah replied that he assumed your 30 per cent already reflected full mastery. Someone else will have that mastery too, Varma said, and give everything. Even podcasting, once his side gig, became his main gig.
~ He could think of no one he knew who had built a successful business while being detached about it.

quote.text: I’m assuming that you’ve reached that level of knowledge where your thirty percent actually is full mastery of something.

sections.label: Love over like
sections.head: Better loved than liked
sections.caption: love over like
body: Thinking about scale too early is dangerous, Amit Varma said. His first rule, put into words by Paul Graham, is that a hundred people who love your product beat a million who like it. {102-C07}

He learnt it on *The Seen and the Unseen*. He used to say he would rather have a hundred thousand people download an episode than ten million watch a YouTube show, where average view times can be fifteen or twenty seconds.

When he checked, his average session was forty minutes, and people listened across multiple sessions. “That is so off the charts that if you told me this fifteen years ago when I was an internet professional, I would just have assumed you’re lying.” {102-S05}
## Slow down to please
Jan Koum, in an interview Varma thinks was with Sam Altman, explained why early WhatsApp charged a dollar: “we didn’t want it to grow too fast.” {102-S02}
The team wanted users it could handle and please, with faster servers and more responsive customer service, before going to the next stage. Varma found that “really inspiring”.
~ Get concrete, he advised: speak to your customers directly and work on what they want. Too often, he said, we retreat into numbers and markets.

quote.text: it’s better to be loved by a few than liked by many.

sections.label: Naysayers
sections.head: The trouble with ‘no, but’
sections.caption: ignoring the naysayers
body: Many people never take the leap, Amit Varma said, because they listen to sceptical voices. Whenever we hear something new, our instinct is to say “no, but”. He consciously stops himself before responding. {#nobut}

Customer focus groups, he said, are the worst way to test a new idea. The telephone was first imagined as a way for telegraph operators to talk to each other, and even Silicon Valley’s media doubted the internet in the 1990s.
## Who to ignore
Think about naysayers that way, Varma urged: the better your idea, the more likely it is that many people will tell you it cannot be done. {102-C08}
Steve Jobs had utter contempt for consultants, he said, because they have no skin in the game. {102-R15}

Vinod Khosla, the founder of Sun Microsystems turned venture capitalist, once said that seventy per cent of VCs add negative value to a company. {#khosla} Unless you have lived through a founder’s daily crises, Varma said, you simply don’t know.
~ A founder who has lived with an idea, kept awake by it at night, should take that conviction far more seriously than outside advice.

quote.text: hire the best people, and then ignore the freaking consultants because they don’t have skin in the game.

sections.label: From inside
sections.head: Never mind the gap
sections.caption: starting from inside
body: “Whatever you do should come from inside, not from outside,” Amit Varma said. Hunting for a gap in the market sends you where everyone else is rushing, which is a path to mediocrity. {102-C09}
Instead, he cited Paul Graham’s advice: just learn. Gain domain expertise, and projects will emerge.

Most great companies, he said, began as projects or hobbies. Yahoo was a web directory for Stanford. Page and Brin started with PageRank, a puzzle about doing search better, and tried to sell it to other search engines. “They weren’t thinking of a business at the time. They were thinking of a pain point.” {102-S06}
## Only you

Peter Thiel’s rule is to work on something that wouldn’t happen without you. That need not mean Mars, Varma said: his long conversations on *The Seen and the Unseen* would not exist without him. {#longform}

Ajay Shah applied the rule by triage. After a bomb goes off at a coffee shop, first responders sort people into green, who will survive anyway, black, who will die, and red, where effort counts most. {102-C11}
~ His laptop is full of half-page scribbles, and he picks a few big battles only he can fight. If you are doing what many others could, he said, you are probably not delegating enough.

quote.text: The red is where you put the peak effort because your impact will be the highest, your marginal contribution will be the highest.

sections.label: Bias for action
sections.head: A road made step by step
sections.caption: the bias for action
body: The episode ended at the beginning, Amit Varma said: with starting. Life is a trade-off between getting it done and getting it right, and too often we plan and plan and never start.
Brian Armstrong of Coinbase puts it in three words: action produces information. Every time you do something, you learn a little. {102-R26}
Kevin Systrom’s biggest regret about Instagram, Varma said, was a private beta that ran for six months or so. The advice: “Don’t do private beta. Just put your product out there.” {#beta}
## The man in the fog
Armstrong also pictured a foggy mountain: wait at the bottom for the fog to clear and you will be there forever. {#fog}
Varma wondered whether he took it from Milan Kundera’s *Testaments Betrayed*, in which a man in a fog takes one step after another and, with each step, makes his road. {102-J14}
Seeing the past as a clearly mapped road, Varma said, is hindsight bias. Certainty is something you can only have when you look back; looking ahead, we are all in fog. {102-C13}
~ “So, dear listener, have a bias for action,” he concluded. “Start your business.”

quote.text: when you’re looking ahead, we are all in fog, and the only way to navigate that fog is to move forward.

side.boxText: Much of Amit Varma’s advice came from clips of founders and investors on StartUp Archive, an Instagram account he calls awesome. Paul Graham, who started Y Combinator, recurs throughout: love over like, compress your working life, just learn. {102-R09}

contQuote.text: So if you’re an entrepreneur with an idea, you’ve been living with that idea, it’s kept you awake at night, you’ve got to take yourself and your passion much, much more seriously than advice coming from outside.

p3.title: Founders’ tales
p3.deck: Four stories Amit Varma told, and what each teaches a would-be founder

stories.start: Like Brian Chesky of Airbnb talks about how he took these words to heart.
stories.end: Chesky's himself landed up with a camera to take the cool photographs.
stories.caption: the founder at the door
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how Airbnb’s founder served his first hosts
stories.head: Ding-dong, Airbnb calling
body: In the early days of Airbnb, when it had only a few customers, Brian Chesky went to see them himself: what was each place like, and what was its owner advertising about it? {102-R10}
Amit Varma told the story to illustrate Paul Graham’s rule that it is better to be loved by a few than liked by many. Chesky, he said, took those words to heart.

Chesky noticed that when hosts photographed their own places, the pictures looked bad. So he asked one of them: would it help if there were a button on the site that sent a photographer over to shoot the place? The host said yes.
A little while after leaving, Chesky called. “Hey, we’ve put a button,” he said, in Varma’s telling. The host clicked it.

“And the next day the doorbell rings, the guy opens it, is Brian Chesky,” Varma said. The host was astonished: “Oh my God, you must be a really small company. Don’t you have anything better to do?” {102-S01}
Chesky himself had landed up with a camera to take the photographs.

It doesn’t matter how many customers you have at the start, Varma said, if each of them loves you. Talk to each of them. Ask how you can improve things. If they want a feature, build it just for them.
~ Once a hundred people love it, the product becomes so good that it begins to spread, and then, he said, scaling isn’t difficult.
stories.why: With only a few customers, a founder can serve each one personally and build exactly what they ask for. A hundred people who love the product will spread it, and then scaling is easy. {102-C07}

stories.start: And the best example that I really love is about cars.
stories.end: we need better bred horses, faster horses. And not that we need a car.
stories.caption: the red flag law
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on an old British law for early cars
stories.head: Three men and a motor car
body: The first car, Amit Varma said, was not greeted as the future of humanity. It was seen as a toy for rich people, who would also hire a driver.
Early cars stopped after a couple of minutes, so each needed a stoker to start the engine again. Even the word, Varma noted, came from an older technology.

Then Britain came up with the red flag law, which required three people for every car. “One is a stoker who’s got to start the engine when it stops, not if. The second is the driver.” The third walked sixty metres ahead of the car, waving a red flag so that horses and carriages didn’t get into trouble. {102-S04}
~ Had Henry Ford surveyed customers, Varma said, people in transportation would have asked for “better bred horses, faster horses”. {102-J11}

quote.text: So this is how outlandish the idea of driving seemed.

stories.start: Like there's a beautiful clip uh we'll link to here
stories.end: But luckily someone took that leap. The show happened.
stories.caption: the Seinfeld pilot
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a test audience that got it badly wrong
stories.head: The pilot nobody wanted back
body: In 1989, a pilot of *Seinfeld* was shown to a test audience. Amit Varma told the story from a clip of Jerry Seinfeld himself. {102-R12}

The verdicts were brutal. “One piece of feedback I remember was, No segment of the audience wants to see the show again,” Varma said. Another said they didn’t like Jerry’s backup ensemble, the cast Varma calls “the greatest”. {102-S03}
Had the marketing people won the argument, the show would never have happened. Luckily, someone took the leap.

~ Varma asked Ajay Shah whether he had watched *Seinfeld*, then assured him that between them they had watched it an average number of times, since Varma had probably watched it twice as much as the normal person. {102-J04}
stories.why: Focus groups and market surveys judge the new against what already exists, so they tend to reject the genuinely new. The better your idea, Varma said, the more people will tell you it cannot be done. {102-C08}

stories.start: there's another great interview of Drew Houston, the founder of Dropbox
stories.end: just having our focus on doing one thing and getting that right
stories.caption: Dropbox’s big bet
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a founder who took a lesson from Intel
stories.head: All the chips in one basket
body: Drew Houston’s Dropbox reached an inflection point, Amit Varma said. It was building video-sharing and file-sharing software, great products both, and it was all over the place. {102-R24}

Then Houston read *Only the Paranoid Survive* by Andy Grove of Intel. Grove describes how early Intel, faring poorly in a relatively saturated market for memory chips, got the chance to make microprocessors, and reached a similar point. {102-R25}
The conclusion, as Varma voiced it: “I need to focus. I need to go all in. I need to put all my chips in one basket.” {102-S09}
~ Dropbox dropped the video side entirely, including, if Varma remembered correctly, a couple of companies it had acquired for it.
stories.why: Focus can mean abandoning good products you have already invested in. Many shiny objects attract us, Varma said, but he is much more in favour of figuring one thing out and getting that right.

quiz.q: What did James C. Scott call the most powerful fertiliser, in the line Ajay Shah quoted?
quiz.a: The tender gaze of an owner: you work better when it is yours.

quiz.q: Why did early WhatsApp charge its users a dollar, according to Jan Koum as Amit Varma recalled?
quiz.a: To slow its growth, so it could please the users it already had.

quiz.q: Under Britain’s red flag law, which three people did every car need?
quiz.a: A stoker to restart the engine, a driver, and a man with a flag.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s triage, what do the green, black and red labels mean after a blast?
quiz.a: Green will survive anyway, black will die, red is where effort matters most.

quiz.q: What did Bill Gates find when Warren Buffett opened his calendar to set up an event?
quiz.a: It was almost blank, because Buffett had learned to say no.

quiz.q: In Milan Kundera’s image, what does an onlooker fail to see when looking back at the man?
quiz.a: The fog: he sees the man and the road, but not the fog.
